Apple__Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is a fungal disease caused by Venturia inaequalis. It is one of the most common and serious diseases of apple trees, thriving in cool and moist spring conditions.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on leaves
Distorted, curled, or twisted leaves in severe infections
Dark, scabby, corky lesions on fruit surface
Premature leaf and fruit drop
remedies: Apply fungicides (myclobutanil, captan, or mancozeb) starting at bud break
Remove and destroy fallen infected leaves to reduce overwintering spores
Prune trees to improve air circulation
Plant resistant apple varieties such as Liberty or Enterprise

Apple__Black_rot.description: Black rot is a fungal disease of apples caused by Botryosphaeria obtusa. It affects fruit, leaves, and bark, and is most severe in warm and humid conditions.
symptoms: Circular brown spots with purple borders on leaves (frog-eye leaf spot)
Rotting fruit turning black and shriveling into mummies
Reddish-brown cankers on branches and trunk
Premature fruit drop
remedies: Prune and destroy infected branches and mummified fruit
Apply captan or thiophanate-methyl fungicides
Avoid wounding the tree during pruning
Maintain tree vigor through proper fertilization and watering

Apple__Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar apple rust is caused by the fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae. It requires two hosts — apple and eastern red cedar — to complete its life cycle.
symptoms: Bright orange-yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces
Tube-like structures (aecia) on the underside of infected leaves
Deformed or spotted fruit
Premature defoliation in heavy infections
remedies: Remove nearby eastern red cedar or juniper trees if possible
Apply fungicides (myclobutanil or triadimefon) from pink bud through petal fall
Plant rust-resistant apple varieties
Monitor and treat early before spore release

Apple__healthy.description: Your apple plant is healthy and showing no signs of disease or pest damage. The leaves, bark, and fruit appear normal and vigorous.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
Leaves are green, firm, and properly shaped
No spots, lesions, or discoloration visible
remedies: Great job! Keep up your current care routine
Water at the base and avoid wetting foliage to prevent fungal issues
Inspect regularly for early signs of apple scab or rust, especially in spring

Blueberry__healthy.description: Your blueberry plant is healthy and thriving with no visible signs of disease or stress.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
Leaves are green and glossy with no spots or curling
Stems and branches look firm and undamaged
remedies: Excellent! Continue your current care routine
Maintain soil pH between 4.5 and 5.5 for optimal nutrient uptake
Keep an eye out for mummy berry disease and powdery mildew in humid seasons

Cherry__Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew on cherry is caused by Podosphaera clandestina. It thrives in warm days with cool nights and high humidity, commonly affecting young tissue.
symptoms: White powdery coating on leaves, shoots, and fruit
Curling, twisting, or stunting of new growth
Premature leaf drop in severe cases
Russeting or scarring on fruit surface
remedies: Apply sulfur-based or potassium bicarbonate fungicides at first sign
Prune trees to improve air circulation and reduce humidity
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which promotes soft new growth
Use resistant cherry varieties where available

Cherry__healthy.description: Your cherry plant is healthy with no visible symptoms of disease, pest damage, or nutrient deficiency.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
Leaves are deep green and smooth with no spots or curling
Branches and bark appear clean and undamaged
remedies: Well done! Your plant is in great shape
Prune annually after harvest to maintain good airflow through the canopy
Watch for powdery mildew or brown rot during warm and humid weather

Corn__Cercospora_leaf_spot_Gray_leaf_spo.description: Gray leaf spot is caused by the fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis. It is a major foliar disease of corn, particularly damaging in warm, humid, and cloudy conditions.
symptoms: Rectangular, tan to gray lesions restricted by leaf veins
Lesions run parallel to the leaf margin
Severe blighting of lower leaves progressing upward
Yield loss due to early death of photosynthetic tissue
remedies: Plant resistant or tolerant corn hybrids
Apply foliar fungicides (strobilurins or triazoles) at early tassel stage
Till or bury crop residue to reduce inoculum
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops

Corn__Common_rust.description: Common rust of corn is caused by Puccinia sorghi. It is widespread in cool, moist conditions and can significantly reduce yield in susceptible hybrids.
symptoms: Small, circular to elongated brick-red pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture to release powdery orange-red spores
Yellowing of leaves around pustules
Premature senescence in severe infections
remedies: Plant rust-resistant corn hybrids
Apply triazole or strobilurin fungicides if infection is early and severe
Scout fields regularly, especially during cool and wet periods
Avoid late planting which increases disease risk

Corn__Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern leaf blight is caused by Exserohilum turcicum. It is one of the most important foliar diseases of corn, thriving in moderate temperatures with high humidity.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, grayish-green to tan cigar-shaped lesions on leaves
Lesions can reach 15–20 cm in length
Dark green sooty appearance when sporulating
Severe blighting reduces photosynthesis and grain fill
remedies: Use resistant corn hybrids with Ht genes
Apply foliar fungicides (azoxystrobin, propiconazole) at tasseling if needed
Rotate crops and till residue to reduce spore load
Avoid dense plant populations that trap moisture

Corn__healthy.description: Your corn plant is healthy and growing well with no signs of fungal, bacterial, or pest-related damage.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
Leaves are broad, green, and free of lesions or discoloration
Stalks are firm and upright with no signs of rot
remedies: Your corn is looking great — keep it up!
Maintain adequate nitrogen levels for strong leaf development
Scout weekly during humid weather for early signs of gray leaf spot or rust

Grape__Black_rot.description: Grape black rot is caused by the fungus Guignardia bidwellii. It is one of the most destructive diseases of grapes in humid climates, affecting leaves, shoots, and fruit.
symptoms: Small reddish-brown circular spots on leaves with dark borders
Tiny black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) in the center of leaf spots
Infected berries shrivel and turn into hard black mummies
Shoot and tendril lesions with black margins
remedies: Apply fungicides (mancozeb, myclobutanil) starting at bud break through veraison
Remove and destroy mummified berries and infected shoots
Improve canopy management to increase air circulation and light
Avoid overhead irrigation

Grape__Esca_(Black_Measles).description: Esca, also called Black Measles, is a complex wood disease of grapevines caused by several fungi including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Phaeoacremonium spp.
symptoms: Tiger-stripe pattern of yellow or red discoloration between leaf veins
Small dark spots or measles on berry skin
Sudden wilting and drying of shoots in summer (apoplexy)
Internal wood browning and decay in trunk and cordons
remedies: Remove and destroy severely infected vines
Protect pruning wounds with fungicidal paste (thiophanate-methyl based)
Prune during dry weather to minimize wound infection
No curative chemical treatment exists; focus on prevention

Grape__Leaf_blight_Isariopsis_Leaf_Spot.description: Grape leaf blight caused by Isariopsis clavispora (also known as Cercospora viticola) is a fungal disease that mainly affects leaves under warm and wet conditions.
symptoms: Irregular dark brown lesions on older leaves
Lesions have a yellowish halo and may coalesce
Premature defoliation in severe cases
Reduced photosynthesis weakening the vine
remedies: Apply copper-based fungicides or mancozeb preventively
Remove fallen and infected leaves from the vineyard floor
Improve air circulation through canopy management
Avoid overhead irrigation and reduce leaf wetness duration

Grape__healthy.description: Your grapevine is healthy and vigorous with no visible signs of disease, mildew, or pest damage.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
Leaves are green, flat, and free of spots or powdery coating
Shoots and tendrils appear strong and undamaged
remedies: Fantastic! Your vine is in great condition
Continue canopy management to ensure good sunlight and airflow
Apply preventive copper sprays before rainy seasons to guard against downy mildew

Orange__Haunglongbing_Citrus_greening.description: Huanglongbing (HLB), also known as citrus greening, is caused by the bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, spread by the Asian citrus psyllid. It is considered the most destructive citrus disease worldwide.
symptoms: Asymmetric yellowing of leaves (blotchy mottle pattern)
Small, lopsided, bitter fruit that remains green at the bottom
Premature fruit drop and twig dieback
Stunted growth and overall tree decline over time
remedies: Control the Asian citrus psyllid vector with insecticides (imidacloprid, organophosphates)
Remove and destroy infected trees to prevent spread
Use certified disease-free planting material
No cure exists; focus on prevention and vector management

Peach__Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot of peach is caused by Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. It is a serious disease in warm and rainy climates, affecting leaves, fruit, and twigs.
symptoms: Small water-soaked spots on leaves turning angular and purple-brown
Shot-hole appearance as infected leaf tissue falls out
Sunken, dark, water-soaked lesions on fruit
Twig cankers leading to dieback
remedies: Apply copper-based bactericides from bud swell through petal fall
Plant resistant peach varieties
Avoid overhead irrigation to reduce leaf wetness
Prune out infected twigs during dry weather

Peach__healthy.description: Your peach plant is healthy with no signs of bacterial spot, leaf curl, or any other common peach disease.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
Leaves are green, smooth, and free of spots or shot-holes
Branches and twigs show no cankers or dieback
remedies: Your peach plant looks great — keep doing what you're doing!
Apply a preventive copper spray before the rainy season each year
Thin fruit clusters to reduce disease pressure and improve fruit size

Pepper__bell__Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot of pepper is caused by Xanthomonas euvesicatoria. It is one of the most devastating diseases of pepper in warm, wet climates.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked circular spots on leaves with yellow halos
Spots turn brown and necrotic, causing shot-hole appearance
Raised, scabby lesions on fruit
Severe defoliation and fruit blemishing reducing marketability
remedies: Apply copper bactericides combined with mancozeb on a preventive schedule
Use certified disease-free or treated seed
Avoid working in the field when plants are wet
Rotate crops and avoid planting peppers or tomatoes in the same area for 2 years

Pepper__bell__healthy.description: Your bell pepper plant is healthy and showing strong growth with no signs of bacterial, fungal, or viral disease.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
Leaves are dark green, flat, and free of spots or blistering
Stems are firm with no lesions or discoloration
remedies: Looking great! Continue your regular care routine
Ensure consistent watering to prevent blossom end rot
Monitor for aphids and whiteflies which can spread viruses to pepper plants

Potato__Early_blight.description: Early blight of potato is caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. It is a common and widespread disease, primarily affecting older leaves under warm and humid conditions.
symptoms: Small dark brown spots with concentric rings giving a target-board appearance
Lesions appear first on older, lower leaves
Yellow tissue surrounding the spots
Severe defoliation reducing tuber yield
remedies: Apply mancozeb or chlorothalonil fungicides starting at early canopy closure
Use certified disease-free seed potatoes
Ensure adequate fertilization especially nitrogen to maintain plant vigor
Rotate crops and destroy infected debris after harvest

Potato__Late_blight.description: Late blight is caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans — the pathogen responsible for the Irish Potato Famine of the 1840s. It spreads rapidly in cool, wet conditions.
symptoms: Water-soaked, pale-green lesions on leaves that rapidly turn brown
White cottony sporulation on the underside of leaves during humid conditions
Dark, greasy-looking lesions on stems
Brown rot extending into tubers with a reddish-brown granular decay
remedies: Apply fungicides containing metalaxyl, mancozeb, or cymoxanil on a regular preventive schedule
Destroy volunteer potato plants and cull piles that harbor the pathogen
Hill soil around plants to protect tubers from spores washing down
Use resistant varieties and certified seed potatoes

Potato__healthy.description: Your potato plant is healthy with no visible signs of early blight, late blight, or any other common potato disease.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
Leaves are green and upright with no spots, lesions, or wilting
Stems are firm and free of dark lesions or rot
remedies: Your potato plant is doing well — keep it up!
Hill soil around the base of plants to protect tubers from sunlight and disease
Scout weekly for late blight during cool and wet periods as it can spread rapidly

Raspberry__healthy.description: Your raspberry plant is healthy and vigorous with no visible signs of disease, cane damage, or pest infestation.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
Leaves are green and free of spots, rust, or discoloration
Canes are firm and show no signs of blight or canker
remedies: Great work — your raspberry plant is thriving!
Remove old fruiting canes after harvest to reduce disease pressure next season
Watch for gray mold during wet weather, especially around ripening fruit

Soybean__healthy.description: Your soybean plant is healthy and growing well with no signs of fungal, bacterial, or viral disease.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
Leaves are green, trifoliate, and free of lesions or yellowing
Stems are firm with no discoloration or rot at the base
remedies: Your soybean crop is in excellent condition — keep it up!
Rotate with non-legume crops each season to maintain soil health
Monitor for sudden death syndrome and Asian soybean rust during humid conditions

Squash__Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew of squash is caused by Podosphaera xanthii (formerly Sphaerotheca fuliginea). It is one of the most common diseases of cucurbits worldwide, thriving in warm days and cool nights.
symptoms: White powdery fungal growth on upper and lower leaf surfaces
Yellowing and browning of affected leaves
Stunted plant growth in severe cases
Premature leaf senescence reducing fruit development
remedies: Apply potassium bicarbonate, sulfur, or neem oil at first sign of infection
Use resistant squash varieties
Improve air circulation through proper plant spacing
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization

Strawberry__Leaf_scorch.description: Strawberry leaf scorch is caused by the fungus Diplocarpon earlianum. It is a common disease in humid regions and can significantly defoliate plants if not managed.
symptoms: Small irregular purplish spots on upper leaf surfaces
Spots enlarge and centers turn brown while margins stay purple
Severely infected leaves appear scorched or burned
Premature defoliation weakening plants and reducing yield
remedies: Apply myclobutanil or captan fungicides starting in early spring
Remove and destroy infected leaves and plant debris
Avoid overhead irrigation to reduce leaf wetness
Plant resistant strawberry varieties and practice crop rotation

Strawberry__healthy.description: Your strawberry plant is healthy and showing no signs of leaf scorch, gray mold, or any other common strawberry disease.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
Leaves are green, firm, and free of purple spots or scorching
Runners and crowns appear clean and undamaged
remedies: Wonderful — your strawberry plant looks perfectly healthy!
Renovate beds after harvest by mowing old leaves to reduce disease carryover
Avoid overhead watering to keep foliage dry and prevent gray mold

Tomato__Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot of tomato is caused by Xanthomonas vesicatoria and related species. It is a significant disease in warm, wet climates affecting leaves, stems, and fruit.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked, circular spots on leaves with yellow halos
Spots turn dark brown and cause shot-hole appearance
Raised, scabby, dark lesions on green fruit
Severe defoliation exposing fruit to sunscald
remedies: Use copper-based bactericides combined with mancozeb preventively
Start with disease-free or hot-water treated seed
Avoid overhead irrigation and working in wet fields
Rotate tomatoes with non-solanaceous crops for 2–3 years

Tomato__Early_blight.description: Early blight of tomato is caused by Alternaria solani. It primarily attacks older leaves and is favored by alternating wet and dry periods with warm temperatures.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings forming a target-board pattern
Yellow halo surrounding each lesion
Infected leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely
Stem lesions near the soil line causing collar rot in seedlings
remedies: Apply chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper fungicides every 7–10 days
Remove infected lower leaves promptly
Mulch around plants to prevent soil splash spreading spores
Rotate crops and avoid planting tomatoes in the same spot for 2–3 years

Tomato__Late_blight.description: Tomato late blight is caused by Phytophthora infestans. It spreads explosively under cool and wet conditions and can destroy an entire crop within days if untreated.
symptoms: Pale green, water-soaked lesions on leaves turning dark brown rapidly
White fuzzy mold on the underside of leaves in humid conditions
Dark, oily lesions on stems
Brown, firm rot on fruit starting from the shoulder
remedies: Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or metalaxyl on a preventive schedule
Remove and bag infected plant tissue to prevent spore spread
Stake plants and prune lower leaves to improve airflow
Use late-blight-resistant tomato varieties

Tomato__Leaf_Mold.description: Tomato leaf mold is caused by the fungus Passalora fulva (formerly Fulvia fulva). It thrives in high humidity and is especially common in greenhouse-grown tomatoes.
symptoms: Pale greenish-yellow spots on the upper leaf surface
Olive-green to grayish-purple velvety mold on the underside of leaves
Infected leaves curl, wither, and drop
Fruit infection is rare but causes dark leathery rot near the stem
remedies: Improve greenhouse ventilation to reduce humidity below 85%
Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper) preventively
Remove and destroy infected leaves
Plant resistant tomato varieties with Cf resistance genes

Tomato__Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot is caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici. It is one of the most common foliar diseases of tomato, appearing first on lower leaves.
symptoms: Small, circular spots with white or gray centers and dark brown borders
Tiny black dots (pycnidia) visible in the center of spots
Yellowing around spots leading to premature leaf drop
Disease progresses upward from lower to upper leaves
remedies: Apply chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper fungicide at first sign
Remove and destroy infected lower leaves
Stake and mulch plants to prevent soil splash
Practice crop rotation and remove plant debris after season

Tomato__Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_.description: Two-spotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae) is a common pest of tomatoes. It thrives in hot, dry conditions and can cause severe damage by sucking cell contents from leaves.
symptoms: Fine yellow stippling or bronzing on upper leaf surfaces
Fine webbing on the underside of leaves and between stems
Leaves become dry, brittle, and eventually drop
Severe infestations cause overall plant decline and yield loss
remedies: Apply miticides (abamectin, spiromesifen) or insecticidal soap
Increase humidity around plants as mites prefer dry conditions
Introduce predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis) for biological control
Avoid excessive nitrogen and water stress which favor mite outbreaks

Tomato__Target_Spot.description: Target spot of tomato is caused by the fungus Corynespora cassiicola. It affects leaves, stems, and fruit, and is common in warm, humid tropical and subtropical regions.
symptoms: Brown circular spots with concentric rings resembling a target on leaves
Spots have yellow halos and may coalesce causing large blighted areas
Small, sunken dark lesions on fruit
Severe defoliation in advanced stages
remedies: Apply fungicides such as azoxystrobin or chlorothalonil preventively
Improve air circulation by pruning lower leaves and proper spacing
Avoid overhead irrigation and wet foliage
Rotate tomatoes with unrelated crops

Tomato__Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV) is a begomovirus transmitted by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). It is one of the most damaging viruses of tomato worldwide.
symptoms: Upward curling and yellowing of leaf margins
Leaves become small, crumpled, and cupped
Stunted plant growth and reduced fruit set
Flowers drop before fruit can develop
remedies: Control whitefly populations with imidacloprid, pymetrozine, or insecticidal soap
Use reflective mulch to repel whiteflies
Plant TYLCV-resistant tomato varieties
Remove and destroy infected plants promptly to prevent spread

Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) is a tobamovirus that spreads through contact with infected plant sap, contaminated tools, and hands. It can persist in soil and plant debris for long periods.
symptoms: Mosaic pattern of light and dark green on leaves
Leaf distortion, blistering, and fern-leaf appearance
Stunted plant growth
Yellow streaks or mottling on fruit
remedies: Use certified virus-free or treated seed
Disinfect tools with 10% bleach solution between plants
Wash hands thoroughly before handling plants
Remove and destroy infected plants; there is no chemical cure

Tomato__healthy.description: Your tomato plant is healthy and thriving with no visible signs of disease, virus, or pest damage.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
Leaves are deep green, firm, and properly shaped with no spots or curling
Stems are strong and free of lesions or discoloration
remedies: Your tomato plant is in great shape — well done!
Water consistently at the base to prevent blossom end rot and fungal splash
Scout weekly for early blight, late blight, and whiteflies, especially in warm and humid weather
